items.title: A byte-level BPE tokeniser
items.prose: Build the whole tokeniser as one class, from a blank start. `train(text, n_merges)` learns merges with our rules. Count overlapping pairs on the current ids and take the most frequent, the first on a tie. Give it id `256 + k`, and stop early when no pair appears twice. Store the merges, pairs of ids from id 256 on, in `self.merges`; a new call replaces them.
items.question: Write `BPETokenizer` with `train(text, n_merges)`, `encode(text)` returning a list of ids, and `decode(ids)` returning a string (decode with `errors='replace'`).

examples.setup: t = BPETokenizer(); t.train('bid bids bidder bidding', 10)
t = BPETokenizer(); t.train('bid bids bidder bidding', 10)

tests.setup: t = BPETokenizer(); t.train('bid bids bidder bidding', 10)
t = BPETokenizer(); t.train('bid bids bidder bidding', 10)
t = BPETokenizer(); t.train('bid bids bidder bidding', 10)
t = BPETokenizer(); t.train('bid bids bidder bidding', 2)
t = BPETokenizer(); t.train('£5 £6 £7 \U0001F4C8\U0001F4C8', 5); s = 'Up £5 \U0001F4C8, €3 and 日本'
t = BPETokenizer(); t.train('bid bids', 5); t.train('toto koko', 5)
text = open('tiny-shakespeare.txt').read(); t = BPETokenizer(); t.train(text[:20000], 50); held = text[-5000:]; ids = t.encode(held)
tests.call: [len(t.merges), t.decode(ids) == held, len(held.encode('utf-8')) / len(ids) > 1.4, t.encode('there whether')]

widget.how: Submit runs 11 hidden tests. They cover the toy merges with their encoding and decoding, the tie in `toto koko`, a cap of 2 merges, and texts with no repeated pair or no text. Others try a run of a's, round trips with £, € and an emoji, and a second `train` that replaces the first. The last learns 50 merges on the first 20,000 Shakespeare characters and scores the last 5,000: a round trip, more than 1.4 bytes per token, and the ids of `there whether`.

mutants.symptom: Breaks ties by the smallest pair, not the first one seen.
A second train keeps the first run's merges.
Encodes by frequency in the new text instead of replaying merges in training order.

feedback.correct: Your tokeniser trains, encodes and decodes as ours does, and compresses held-out Shakespeare.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-4: Test 4 is a tie: `to` and `ko` both appear twice. Take the pair that occurs first in the text.
byKey.test-10: Test 10 trains twice on one object. The second `train` must start from fresh merges.
byKey.test-11: Test 11 learns 50 merges on Shakespeare and needs more than 1.4 bytes per token on held-out text. Check that `encode` replays every merge in order.

explain.text: `train` is the loop of count, choose, merge; `encode` replays the merges in order; `decode` expands ids to bytes. On held-out Shakespeare, 50 merges give about 1.44 bytes per token.

items.title: Flag near-duplicate headlines
items.prose: A news feed repeats stories with small edits. Two headlines are near duplicates when the Jaccard similarity of their sets of 5-character shingles is at least `threshold`. A text shorter than 5 characters has no shingles and is never flagged.
items.question: Write `near_duplicates(docs, threshold)`, returning every flagged pair as `[i, j]` with `i < j`, ordered by `i` then `j`.

widget.prelude: HEADLINES = ['Calder Foods lifts full-year profit guidance after strong summer trading', 'Calder Foods lifts full-year profit guidance after strong summer trading.', 'Calder Foods lifts full-year profit guidance after strong winter trading', 'Brightwater Utilities cuts its dividend as costs rise', 'Brightwater Utilities cuts its dividend as costs rise sharply', 'Calder Foods names a new chief executive', 'Q3']
widget.how: Submit runs 8 hidden tests. They try identical texts, and the seven headlines in `HEADLINES` (defined for you) at thresholds 0.8, 0.9 and 0.5. Others have texts too short for a shingle, an empty list, a threshold of 1, and a pair exactly at its threshold.

mutants.symptom: Flags only pairs strictly above the threshold.
Divides by zero when two texts have no shingles.
Divides by the larger set instead of the union.

feedback.correct: Your filter flags exactly the near copies at every threshold.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-5: Test 5 has texts under 5 characters. Their shingle sets are empty; never flag them.
byKey.test-8: Test 8 sits exactly on the threshold. Flag a pair when its similarity is at least the threshold.

explain.text: Build each shingle set once, then compare every pair with $i < j$. A headline with a full stop added shares almost every shingle; one with a different season shares fewer.

items.title: One merge, step by step
items.prose: Put the steps of one round of BPE training in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.
items.question: Order the steps.

lines.text: Count every pair of neighbours in the current ids, overlaps included
Choose the pair with the highest count; on a tie, the one that occurs first
Stop training if that count is below 2
Give the pair the next new id, 256 plus the merges made so far
Scan left to right, replacing each occurrence and jumping past both ids
Append the pair to the merge list
Recount the pairs on the original bytes of the text
lines.why: Counts come from the current ids. The original bytes still hold pairs that earlier merges have swallowed.

feedback.correct: Count, choose, check, name, replace, record.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Each step needs what the one before produced.

byKey.d1: Counts come from the current ids, never the original bytes.
byKey.left-out: Every step but one belongs; put the left-out one back.

explain.text: We count on the current ids, choose the top pair and stop if its count is below 2. Then we give it an id, replace it and record it. Recording may come before or after the replacement.

items.title: Counting letters
items.question: Write your answer as you would explain it to a colleague.

widget.prompt: Chatbots often miscount the letters in a word: asked how many r's are in strawberry, some answer 2. Explain why a language model often fails at this, in terms of tokens. Give an example split and say what helps.
widget.model:
A language model never sees letters. Its input is a list of token ids, and each id stands for a run of bytes chosen by the tokeniser.

**What the model sees.** The tokeniser we trained with 200 merges on the Shakespeare slice splits ` strawberry` into eight tokens: a space, `st`, `ra`, `w`, `b`, `er`, `r`, `y`. A production tokeniser with tens of thousands of merges makes fewer, longer tokens, often two or three for this word. Each id arrives as one number; nothing in the input says that `ra` holds an r.

**Why counting fails.** To count the r's, the model must know the spelling inside each token, add 1 for `ra`, 1 for `er` and 1 for `r`, and keep a running total. Spelling a token is a fact the model can only learn from training text that happens to spell words out; it is weaker for rare tokens. And the model produces its answer one token at a time, so a count that needs several hidden steps is easy to get wrong.

**Why it varies.** The split depends on the exact bytes: a leading space, a capital letter or a plural gives other tokens, so the same question can succeed in one form and fail in another.

**What helps.** Ask the model to write the word one letter per line, or with spaces between the letters, so each letter becomes its own token, and then count. Better still, ask it to run code such as `'strawberry'.count('r')`, which counts characters exactly.

rubric.text: States that the model's input is token ids, each standing for a run of bytes, not letters
Gives a concrete split of a word into multi-letter tokens (for example ` strawberry` into `st`, `ra`, `w`, `b`, `er`, `r`, `y` plus the space)
Explains that letters inside a token are not visible in the input, so spelling must be learned from training text and is weaker for rare tokens
Notes that counting needs several hidden steps while the model emits one token at a time
Notes that the split changes with spaces, capitals or word forms, so results vary
Gives a remedy that works at the letter level: spell the word out letter by letter, or run code

items.title: A loss in bits per byte
items.prose: A model is scored on 2,400,000 bytes of company filings. Its tokeniser turns them into 800,000 tokens, and the model's loss is 2.95 nats per token.
items.question: What is the loss in bits per byte? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: 3 bytes per token, so $2.95 / (3 \ln 2) \approx 1.4187$ bits per byte.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the bytes per token first, then convert.

byKey.no-ln2: That is nats per byte. Divide by $\ln 2$.
byKey.per-token: That is bits per token. Divide by the 3 bytes each token covers.
byKey.tokens-per-byte: You multiplied by the bytes per token. Each token covers 3 bytes, so the loss per byte is a third: divide.

explain.text: $2400000 / 800000 = 3$ bytes per token. Then $2.95 / (3 \ln 2) \approx 1.4187$ bits per byte.

items.title: Checking for a leaked test set
items.prose: A team trains a model on web text and tests it on a set of 2,000 analyst reports. It wants to know whether any test report also sits in the training text.
items.question: Which check finds test reports that leaked, even with a changed header?

options.text: Compare each report's shingles with the training documents' and flag high Jaccard
Hash each report and look for the same hash in training
options.why: An exact hash misses a copy whose header or one figure was changed.

options.text: Compare the total sizes of the test and training sets
options.why: Sizes say nothing about which texts overlap.

options.text: Check whether the test loss is low
options.why: A low loss can come from a good model; it does not show a leak.

feedback.correct: Shingle overlap finds near copies, not only exact ones.
feedback.generic: Not quite. A leaked report may differ in a few characters.

explain.text: A copy with a new header shares almost every shingle with the original, so its Jaccard similarity stays high. An exact hash catches only identical copies.
